t.1.49.1: The Sūta said: Then the serpent-woman Jaratkāru, summoning her own son, spoke these words to him at the bidding of Vāsuki, king of the Nāgas.
t.1.49.2: Son, I was given to your father by my brother for a purpose, and that time has now arrived; therefore do what is right.
t.1.49.4: Then she, Jaratkāru, the sister of the king of the Nāgas, who desired the welfare of her kinsmen, told him, undismayed.
t.1.49.3: Āstīka said: For what reason were you given to my father by my maternal uncle? Tell me that truly; having heard it, I shall act accordingly.
t.1.49.5: Kadrū, it is heard, is the mother of all the serpents. Learn now why her sons were cursed by her in her anger.
t.1.49.7: At the sacrifice of Janamejaya, the one whose charioteer is the wind will burn you; there, having met your dissolution into the five elements, you will go to the world of the dead.
t.1.49.6: Since, my little sons, that king of horses Uccaiḥśravas was not made false for my sake in the wager I made concerning Vinatā, with her enslavement as the stake...
t.1.49.8: And to her, who had cursed thus, the Grandfather of the worlds himself spoke the words, "So be it," and he approved of it.
t.1.49.9: And Vāsuki too, having then heard that word of the Grandfather, went for refuge to the gods, dear son, when the amṛta had been churned.
t.1.49.10: And all the gods, their purpose accomplished, having obtained the supreme amṛta, placed my brother at their head and went to Prajāpati.
t.1.49.11: All the gods, together with King Vāsuki, sought to win the favor of the Grandfather, praying that the curse might not come to pass.
t.1.49.13: Jaratkāru will obtain as his wife a woman named Jaratkāru; the twice-born son born of her will free the serpents from the curse.
t.1.49.12: This Vāsuki, king of the Nāgas, is grieved on account of his kinsmen, thinking, “O blessed one, may that curse pronounced by his mother not come to pass.”
t.1.49.14: Having heard these words, Vāsuki, lord of the serpents, gave me, O you who resemble an immortal, to your great-souled father. Then, long before the appointed time had come, you were born in me.
t.1.49.15: This is that time which has now arrived; you ought to save us from our peril. And so you ought to save my brother as well from that fire.
t.1.49.17: Thus addressed, Āstīka then said "So be it" to his mother, and spoke to Vāsuki, who was tormented by grief, as though restoring him to life.
t.1.49.16: May that deed of ours prove not to be fruitless, namely that I was given to your wise father for the sake of deliverance. Or how do you see it, my son?
t.1.49.18: I shall free you from that curse, O Vāsuki, best of serpents, O great-spirited one; this I tell you truly.
t.1.49.19: Be at ease in your mind, O serpent, for there is no danger for you. I shall strive, gentle one, so that good will come of it. My speech has never uttered a falsehood even in jest, how much less otherwise?
t.1.49.20: Going to that best of kings, Janamejaya, who has been consecrated for the sacrifice, I shall today please him with words full of auspiciousness, O uncle, so that the king's sacrifice will come to an end, O best of the good.
t.1.49.22: Āstīka, I reel and my heart is splitting apart; oppressed by the Brahmin's curse, I can no longer make out the directions.
t.1.49.21: Therefore, O lord of serpents, O wise one, trust in me for everything; the faith your mind has placed in me will never prove false.
t.1.49.23: You must not grieve in any way, O best of serpents. I shall destroy your fear, which has arisen from the blazing fire.
t.1.49.24: I shall destroy the Brahmin's curse, most dreadful and blazing like the fire at the end of time; do not, in any way, give yourself to fear over this.
t.1.49.25: Then he removed the dreadful fever of Vāsuki's mind, took it upon his own limbs, and went off in great haste.
t.1.49.27: Having gone there, Āstīka saw the excellent sacrificial enclosure, surrounded by many assembly-priests whose splendor equaled the sun and fire.
t.1.49.26: To that sacrifice of Janamejaya, endowed with all excellences, Āstīka, the best of the twice-born, went for the deliverance of the lords of the serpents.
t.1.49.28: Stopped there by the doorkeepers as he was entering, that best of brahmins, the most excellent of the twice-born, seeking admission, praised that sacrifice.
